cells.tense: The pen is in your hand right now, and the shapes you draw around things are holding.
cells.ask: Take one shelf, drawer or list you keep — physical, today — and sort it into three piles: finished, still running, carried for someone else. Finish it in one sitting.
cells.core:
The shapes you draw around things are holding. You know what's finished and what's still running, you can put your hand on the right one when someone asks, and things around you settle because you've said where they go. That's what a good shape does — it lets the mess be a mess without letting it be chaos.

What that steadiness is free to feed is the moment before the sorting — the quick pull toward one thing before you can explain why. That pull is the part of you that already knows what to attend to, and it only stays accurate if it's allowed to speak first once in a while. Let it name one thing before the reasoning catches up, and see whether it was right.
cells.sheetLine: You say what goes where, and the saying holds.
cells.verb: Giving a workable shape to what's tangled — sorting what belongs where and holding that shape clear.
cells.place: Where something has finished and has to be let end cleanly so the next thing has room to start.

cells.tense: You're bracing for an ending that hasn't arrived, building the structure for it ahead of time.
cells.ask: Pick one thing that's wrapping up and draw its ending as a timeline on paper — order of steps, who says what, when — then close the notebook and do nothing about it for a day.
cells.core:
You're building the shape for an ending that hasn't arrived. It's ordered, sequenced, thought through in advance — and the grip on it has tightened past the point where it serves what it's holding. Preparing the ending has become a way of bracing, not a way of finishing.

What's worth noticing is that a structure can hold something without gripping it. When you can see the shape under the surface — what's actually ending, in what order, and why — the organizing stops being a way of forecasting and becomes a way of understanding. That kind of seeing frees you from having to stand in a future you can't write in. Name the shape once, without acting on it, and let today stay today.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding the ending so tightly the shape has become the work.
cells.verb: Giving a workable shape to what's tangled — sorting what belongs where and holding that shape clear.
cells.place: Where something has finished and has to be let end cleanly so the next thing has room to start.

cells.tense: The decision that would pull the pieces together was made some time back, and you haven't moved past it.
cells.ask: Write one sentence on paper naming something that is over for you, date it today, and leave it somewhere you'll see it each morning this week.
cells.core:
The pieces are all there and they won't fit together. Something needs to close for the rest to arrange itself, and the closing is what isn't happening. So the days go by with the same unfinished stack in the same place.

Underneath that is usually something true that's been half-noticed and not let count — an ending that could be named in one line and hasn't been. Effort won't force the pieces into shape. What shifts them is a moment of clear seeing, where a false arrangement falls away and what's left turns out to be something decided a while back anyway. That kind of clearing moves fast once it starts.
cells.sheetLine: The pieces are there and the decision that would pull them together isn't.
cells.verb: Giving a workable shape to what's tangled — sorting what belongs where and holding that shape clear.

cells.tense: You're giving things their shape all day long while feeling like nothing about you is fixed.
cells.ask: Pick one call you made this week — what ended or what got cleared — and write one line on paper: 'That one was mine.' Read it once before you close the page.
cells.core:
You give things shape all day long and it doesn't feel like it belongs to you. Others rely on how you hold the line and what you let stand, and inside it feels like there's no line at all — nothing decided, nothing settled, nothing claimed.

What's happening is that endings get made through you and the making goes unrecorded. The way through isn't to organize harder. Start from where the ending was actually felt — the plain recognition that one thing is over and the next is coming — and count those as yours. Sign for the place you already stand, and the shape stops being something that happens to you.
cells.sheetLine: You shape what ends. You just haven't put your name on it.

attempts.check: The one personal claim I can't support from the record is any statement about what a person's life or relationships are like beyond the two facts given: structure is being built, and something in this region is ending. So I've kept the cells to what deciding-then-ending looks like from the inside and left the biography alone; a reader can say 'that's not my situation' and still use the ask. The asks are one visible act each — sort one pile, draw the line, write one ending, mark one calm cut as mine — and each stays useful even if my read is wrong, because the person learns what happened when they did it. The sentence that serves the writer more than the reader is any 'there's a version where it works' line; I've cut those and kept both sides of the picture.
